But if the reader will refer to our remarks on <reference osisRef="Mark.16.7">Mr 16:7</reference>, and <reference osisRef="John.18.27">Joh 18:27</reference>, he will have convincing evidence of a Petrine hand in this Gospel.<div eID="gen26640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26641" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">It remains only to advert, in a word or two, to the readers for whom this Gospel was, in the first instance, designed, and the date of it. That it was not for Jews but Gentiles, is evident from the great number of explanations of Jewish usages, opinions, and places, which to a Jew would at that time have been superfluous, but were highly needful to a Gentile. We can here but refer to <reference osisRef="Mark.2.18">Mr 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.3">7:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.12.18">12:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.13.3">13:3</reference>; 14:12; 15:42, for examples of these. Regarding the date of this Gospel--</hi>about which nothing certain is known--if the tradition reported by Irenæus can be relied on, that it was written at Rome, "after the departure of Peter and Paul," and if by that word "departure" we are to understand their death, we may date it somewhere between the years 64 and 68; but in all likelihood this is too late. It is probably nearer the truth to date it eight or ten years earlier.<div eID="gen26641" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">CHAPTER 1</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.1.1-Mark.1.8">Mr 1:1-8</reference>. The Preaching and Baptism of John. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.3.1-Matt.3.12">Mt 3:1-12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.3.1-Luke.3.18">Lu 3:1-18</reference>).</title> <div sID="gen26642" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13855"/><hi type="bold">1. The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God--</hi>By the "Gospel" of Jesus Christ here is evidently meant the blessed Story which our Evangelist is about to tell of His Life, Ministry, Death, Resurrection, and Glorification, and of the begun Gathering of Believers in His Name. The abruptness with which he announces his subject, and the energetic brevity with which, passing by all preceding events, he hastens over the ministry of John and records the Baptism and Temptation of Jesus--as if impatient to come to the Public Life of the Lord of glory--have often been noticed as characteristic of this Gospel--a Gospel whose direct, practical, and singularly vivid setting imparts to it a preciousness peculiar to itself. What strikes every one is, that though the briefest of all the Gospels, this is in some of the principal scenes of our Lord's history the fullest. But what is not so obvious is, that wherever the finer and subtler feelings of humanity, or the deeper and more peculiar hues of our Lord's character were brought out, these, though they should be lightly passed over by all the other Evangelists, are sure to be found here, and in touches of such quiet delicacy and power, that though scarce observed by the cursory reader, they leave indelible impressions upon all the thoughtful and furnish a key to much that is in the other Gospels. These few opening words of the Second Gospel are enough to show, that though it was the purpose of this Evangelist to record chiefly the outward and palpable facts of our Lord's public life, he recognized in Him, in common with the Fourth Evangelist, the glory of the Only-begotten of the Father. <div eID="gen26642" type="x-p"/>
entries.1784c29d93258884f71e42f62946814602bca9d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13856"/><div sID="gen26643" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13856"/><hi type="bold">2-3. As it is written in the prophets, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee--</hi>(Mal 3:1; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.3">Is 40:3</reference>). <div eID="gen26643" type="x-p"/>
entries.138d1b2c3b725d637910b2988079f6ed53823483: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13858"/><div sID="gen26650" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13858"/><hi type="bold">21. And they went into Capernaum--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="Matt.4.13">Mt 4:13</reference>).<div eID="gen26650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26651" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and straightway on the sabbath day he entered into the synagogue, and taught--</hi>This should have been rendered, "straightway on the sabbaths He entered into the synagogue and taught," or "continued to teach." The meaning is, that as He began this practice on the very first sabbath after coming to settle at Capernaum, so He continued it regularly thereafter. <div eID="gen26651" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea1cc36689e82a2561ee68f8235f6d07720debd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13859"/><div sID="gen26652" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13859"/><hi type="bold">22. And they were astonished at his doctrine--</hi>or "teaching"--referring quite as much to the manner as the matter of it.<div eID="gen26652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26653" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for he taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.7.28">Mt 7:28</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.29">29</reference>. <div eID="gen26653" type="x-p"/>
entries.765ebec47c14cad7c740d03fb550876f5ffe2b2e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13860"/><div sID="gen26654" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13860"/><hi type="bold">23. And there was in their synagogue a man with an unclean spirit--</hi>literally, "in an unclean spirit"--that is, so entirely under demoniacal power that his personality was sunk for the time in that of the spirit. The frequency with which this character of "impurity" is ascribed to evil spirits--some twenty times in the Gospels--is not to be overlooked.<div eID="gen26654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26655" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he cried out--</hi>as follows: <div eID="gen26655" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7e44c6b9f2faf14961acc18d8c149395674304a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13861"/><div sID="gen26656" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13861"/><hi type="bold">24. Saying, Let us alone--</hi>or rather, perhaps, "ah!" expressive of mingled astonishment and terror.<div eID="gen26656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26657" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">what have we to do with thee--</hi>an expression of frequent occurrence in the Old Testament (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.17.18">1Ki 17:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Kgs.3.13">2Ki 3:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.35.21">2Ch 35:21</reference>, &c.). It denotes entire separation of interests:--that is, "Thou and we have nothing in common; we want not Thee; what wouldst Thou with us?" For the analogous application of it by our Lord to His mother, see on <reference osisRef="John.2.4">Joh 2:4</reference>.<div eID="gen26657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26658" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou Jesus of Nazareth--</hi>"Jesus, Nazarene!" an epithet originally given to express contempt, but soon adopted as the current designation by those who held our Lord in honor (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.37">Lu 18:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.16.6">Mr 16:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.2.22">Ac 2:22</reference>).<div eID="gen26658" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26659" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">art thou come to destroy us?--</hi>In the case of the Gadarene demoniac the question was, "Art Thou come hither to torment us before the time?" (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.29">Mt 8:29</reference>). Themselves tormentors and destroyers of their victims, they discern in Jesus their own destined tormentor and destroyer, anticipating and dreading what they know and feel to be awaiting them! Conscious, too, that their power was but permitted and temporary, and perceiving in Him, perhaps, the woman's Seed that was to bruise the head and destroy the works of the devil, they regard His approach to them on this occasion as a signal to let go their grasp of this miserable victim.<div eID="gen26659" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26660" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I know thee who thou art, the Holy One of God--</hi>This and other even more glorious testimonies to our Lord were given, as we know, with no good will, but in hope that, by the acceptance of them, He might appear to the people to be in league with evil spirits--a calumny which His enemies were ready enough to throw out against Him. But a Wiser than either was here, who invariably rejected and silenced the testimonies that came to Him from beneath, and thus was able to rebut the imputations of His enemies against Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.24-Matt.12.30">Mt 12:24-30</reference>). The expression, "Holy One of God," seems evidently taken from that Messianic Psalm (<reference osisRef="Ps.16.10">Psa 16:10</reference>), in which He is styled "Thine Holy One." <div eID="gen26660" type="x-p"/>
entries.6cb68eee4abcb7b85d17d26b861a11b2751317d4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13862"/><div sID="gen26661" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13862"/><hi type="bold">25. And Jesus rebuked him, saying, Hold thy peace, and come out of him--</hi>A glorious word of command. Bengel remarks that it was only the testimony borne to Himself which our Lord meant to silence. That he should afterwards cry out for fear or rage (<reference osisRef="Mark.1.26">Mr 1:26</reference>) He would right willingly permit. <div eID="gen26661" type="x-p"/>
entries.8d13a1e32b3fd7d10d022f0f1ebbafc79a545a1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13863"/><div sID="gen26662" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13863"/><hi type="bold">26. And when the unclean spirit had torn him--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.35">Lu 4:35</reference>) says, "When he had thrown him in the midst." Malignant cruelty--just showing what he would have done, if permitted to go farther: it was a last fling!<div eID="gen26662" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26663" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and cried with a loud voice--</hi>the voice of enforced submission and despair.<div eID="gen26663" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26664" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he came out of him--</hi>Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.35">Lu 4:35</reference>) adds, "and hurt him not." Thus impotent were the malignity and rage of the impure spirit when under the restraint of "the Stronger than the strong one armed" (<reference osisRef="Luke.11.21">Lu 11:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.11.22">22</reference>). <div eID="gen26664" type="x-p"/>
entries.99ccf69e65cd9b16519b7bcf30dd31dcd88bfd9d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13864"/><div sID="gen26665" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13864"/><hi type="bold">27. What thing is this? what new doctrine--</hi>teaching<div eID="gen26665" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26666" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">is this?--</hi>The audience, rightly apprehending that the miracle was wrought to illustrate the teaching and display the character and glory of the Teacher, begin by asking what novel kind of teaching this could be, which was so marvellously attested. <div eID="gen26666" type="x-p"/>
entries.b9bdcf7c136dccb974b3d5c30eaa77955d9c8f0e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13865"/><div sID="gen26667" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13865"/><hi type="bold">28. And immediately his fame spread abroad throughout all the region round about Galilee--</hi>rather, "the whole region of Galilee"; though some, as Meyer and Ellicott, explain it of the country surrounding Galilee. <div eID="gen26667" type="x-p"/>
entries.cfac9fec38ae797626065bd8db1bf8707ef92bab: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13866"/><div sID="gen26668" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13866"/><hi type="bold">29. And forthwith, when they were come out of the synagogue--</hi>so also in <reference osisRef="Luke.4.38">Lu 4:38</reference>.<div eID="gen26668" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26669" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they entered into the house of Simon and Andrew, with James and John--</hi>The mention of these four--which is peculiar to Mark--is the first of those traces of Peter's hand in this Gospel, of which we shall find many more. The house being his, and the illness and cure so nearly affecting himself, it is interesting to observe this minute specification of the number and names of the witnesses; interesting also as the first occasion on which the sacred triumvirate of Peter and James and John are selected from among the rest, to be a threefold cord of testimony to certain events in their Lord's life (see on <reference osisRef="Mark.5.37">Mr 5:37</reference>)--Andrew being present on this occasion, as the occurrence took place in his own house. <div eID="gen26669" type="x-p"/>
entries.6824adbfcfdda72967682e4f192e2223a708d159: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13867"/><div sID="gen26670" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13867"/><hi type="bold">30. But Simon's wife's mother lay sick of a fever--</hi>Luke, as was natural in "the beloved physician" (<reference osisRef="Col.4.14">Col 4:14</reference>), describes it professionally; calling it a "great fever," and thus distinguishing it from that lighter kind which the Greek physicians were wont to call "small fevers," as Galen, quoted by Wetstein, tells us.<div eID="gen26670" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26671" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and anon--</hi>immediately.<div eID="gen26671" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26672" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they tell him of her--</hi>naturally hoping that His compassion and power towards one of His own disciples would not be less signally displayed than towards the demonized stranger in the synagogue. <div eID="gen26672" type="x-p"/>
entries.de01f3a7fb0273ebf1180626d2b8cc2a78c22c4d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13868"/><div sID="gen26673" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13868"/><hi type="bold">31. And he came and took her by the hand--</hi>rather, "And advancing, He took her," &c. The beloved physician again is very specific: "And He stood over her."<div eID="gen26673" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26674" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and lifted her up--</hi>This act of condescension, most felt doubtless by Peter, is recorded only by Mark.<div eID="gen26674" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26675" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and immediately the fever left her, and she ministered unto them--</hi>preparing their sabbath-meal: in token both of the perfectness and immediateness of the cure, and of her gratitude to the glorious Healer. <div eID="gen26675" type="x-p"/>
entries.9bc7942b52a2a225b21e1aa8952a83d16fa49c58: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13869"/><div sID="gen26676" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13869"/><hi type="bold">32. And at even, when the sun did set--</hi>so <reference osisRef="Matt.8.16">Mt 8:16</reference>. Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.40">Lu 4:40</reference>) says it was setting.<div eID="gen26676" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26677" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they brought unto him all that were diseased, and them that were possessed with devils--</hi>the demonized. From <reference osisRef="Luke.13.14">Lu 13:14</reference> we see how unlawful they would have deemed it to bring their sick to Jesus for a cure during the sabbath hours. They waited, therefore, till these were over, and then brought them in crowds. Our Lord afterwards took repeated occasion to teach the people by example, even at the risk of His own life, how superstitious a straining of the sabbath rest this was. <div eID="gen26677" type="x-p"/>
entries.f0d6aa298709137bd5b1c5009a7d6a55ac98eba7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13870"/><div sID="gen26678" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13870"/><hi type="bold">33. And all the city was gathered together at the door--</hi>of Peter's house; that is, the sick and those who brought them, and the wondering spectators. This bespeaks the presence of an eye-witness, and is one of those lively examples of word-painting so frequent in this Gospel. <div eID="gen26678" type="x-p"/>
entries.5390e561f66ae875f95f2b8795d936586f4af8b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13871"/><div sID="gen26679" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13871"/><hi type="bold">34. And he healed many that were sick of divers diseases, and cast out many devils--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Matt.8.16">Mt 8:16</reference> it is said, "He cast out the spirits with His word"; or rather, "with a word"--a word of command.<div eID="gen26679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26680" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and suffered not the devils to speak, because they knew him--</hi>Evidently they would have spoken, if permitted, proclaiming His Messiahship in such terms as in the synagogue; but once in one day, and that testimony immediately silenced, was enough. See on <reference osisRef="Mark.1.24">Mr 1:24</reference>. After this account of His miracles of healing, we have in <reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Mt 8:17</reference> this pregnant quotation, "That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Esaias the prophet, saying (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">Is 53:4</reference>), Himself took our infirmities, and bare our sicknesses." <div eID="gen26680" type="x-p"/>
entries.e065d57c162150b8037950713cd46b51c7fe4b42: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13872"/><div sID="gen26681" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13872"/><hi type="bold">35. And in the morning--</hi>that is, of the day after this remarkable sabbath; or, on the first day of the week. His choosing this day to inaugurate a new and glorious stage of His public work, should be noted by the reader.<div eID="gen26681" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26682" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rising up a great while before day--</hi>"while it was yet night," or long before daybreak.<div eID="gen26682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26683" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he went out--</hi>all unperceived from Peter's house, where He slept.<div eID="gen26683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed--</hi>or, "continued in prayer." He was about to begin His first preaching and healing circuit; and as on similar solemn occasions (<reference osisRef="Luke.5.16">Lu 5:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.6.12">6:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.18">9:18</reference>, 28, 29; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.46">Mr 6:46</reference>), He spent some time in special prayer, doubtless with a view to it. What would one not give to have been, during the stillness of those grey morning hours, within hearing--not of His "strong crying and tears," for He had scarce arrived at the stage for that--but of His calm, exalted anticipations of the work which lay immediately before Him, and the outpourings of His soul about it into the bosom of Him that sent Him! He had doubtless enjoyed some uninterrupted hours of such communings with His heavenly Father ere His friends from Capernaum arrived in search of Him. As for them, they doubtless expected, after such a day of miracles, that the next day would witness similar manifestations. When morning came, Peter, loath to break in upon the repose of his glorious Guest, would await His appearance beyond the usual hour; but at length, wondering at the stillness, and gently coming to see where the Lord lay, he finds it--like the sepulchre afterwards--empty! Speedily a party is made up to go in search of Him, Peter naturally leading the way. <div eID="gen26684" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fac0f4f2cd76f31d01c71b6e10ec3ab4ef06981: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13873"/><div sID="gen26685" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13873"/><hi type="bold">36. And Simon and they that were with him followed after him--</hi>rather, "pressed after Him." Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.42">Lu 4:42</reference>) says, "The multitudes sought after Him"; but this would be a party from the town. Mark, having his information from Peter himself, speaks only of what related directly to him. "They that were with him" would probably be Andrew his brother, James and John, with a few other choice brethren. <div eID="gen26685" type="x-p"/>
entries.2a2232c7a33ffed227d46bf1aedd6e147fd5d789: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13874"/><div sID="gen26686" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13874"/><hi type="bold">37. And when they had found him--</hi>evidently after some search.<div eID="gen26686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26687" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they said unto him, All men seek for thee--</hi>By this time, "the multitudes" who, according to Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.42">Lu 4:42</reference>), "sought after Him"--and who, on going to Peter's house, and there learning that Peter and a few more were gone in search of Him, had set out on the same errand--would have arrived, and "came unto Him and stayed Him, that He should not depart from them" (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.42">Lu 4:42</reference>); all now urging His return to their impatient townsmen. <div eID="gen26687" type="x-p"/>
entries.f89561a43a0c871a2ae9d150649b702a64317320: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13875"/><div sID="gen26688" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13875"/><hi type="bold">38. And he said unto them, Let us go--</hi>or, according to another reading, "Let us go elsewhere."<div eID="gen26688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26689" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into the next towns--</hi>rather, "unto the neighboring village-towns"; meaning those places intermediate between towns and villages, with which the western side of the Sea of Galilee was studded.<div eID="gen26689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26690" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I may preach there also; for therefore came I forth--</hi>not from Capernaum, as De Wette miserably interprets, nor from His privacy in the desert place, as Meyer, no better; but from the Father. Compare <reference osisRef="John.16.28">Joh 16:28</reference>, "I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world," &c.--another proof, by the way, that the lofty phraseology of the Fourth Gospel was not unknown to the authors of the others, though their design and point of view are different. The language in which our Lord's reply is given by Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.43">Lu 4:43</reference>) expresses the high necessity under which, in this as in every other step of His work, He acted--"I <hi type="bold">must preach the kingdom of God to other cities also; for therefore"--</hi>or, "to this end"--"am I sent." An act of self-denial it doubtless was, to resist such pleadings to return to Capernaum. But there were overmastering considerations on the other side. <div eID="gen26690" type="x-p"/> <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13876"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Mark.1.40-Mark.1.45">Mr 1:40-45</reference>. Healing of a Leper. ( = <reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.8.4">Mt 8:1-4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.5.12-Luke.5.16">Lu 5:12-16</reference>).</title> <title type="x-s3">See on <reference osisRef="Matt.8.1-Matt.8.4">Mt 8:1-4</reference>.</title> <div sID="gen26691" type="x-p"/> <chapter eID="Mark.1"/>

entries.cf8f28cde8fd4641223889ed03036c5e09d43c82: <div eID="gen39044" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Preface to the Gospel According to St. Mark With a Short Account of His Life</title> <div sID="gen39045" type="x-p"/> For an explication of the word Gospel, and the title Saint, see the Preface to Matthew. <div eID="gen39045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39046" type="x-p"/> Mark. This person, the second in the commonly received order of the four evangelists, was named John Mark, and was the son of a pious woman called Mary, who dwelt at Jerusalem: she was an early believer, and the disciples used to meet at her house. Peter, having been delivered out of prison by an angel, came to the house of Mary, mother of John, whose surname was Mark, where many were gathered together praying, <reference osisRef="Act.12.12">Act 12:12</reference>. This very first mention of John Mark assures us of Peter's intimacy in that family: it is almost universally allowed that Mark, mentioned by Peter, <reference osisRef="1Pet.5.13">1Pet 5:13</reference>, is this evangelist, and that he is the same with him who is called sister's son to Barnabas, <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, and is supposed to have been converted by Peter to the Christian faith. Mr. W. Whiston supposes him to have been Peter's own son. See his Primitive New Test. Notes at the end. He traveled from Jerusalem to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas, <reference osisRef="Act.12.25">Act 12:25</reference>, and some short time after he accompanied them to other countries as their minister, <reference osisRef="Act.13.5">Act 13:5</reference>. When they returned to the continent, and came on shore at Perga in Pamphylia, he departed from them and returned to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Act.13.13">Act 13:13</reference>. Afterwards he would have gone with Paul and Barnabas, but the former refused to take him, because of his having left them at Pamphylia; Paul and Barnabas then separated, and Mark accompanied his uncle Barnabas to Cyprus, <reference osisRef="Act.15.36-Act.15.41">Act 15:36-41</reference>. Afterwards Paul and he were fully reconciled, as evidently appears from <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.11">2Tim 4:11</reference> : Take Mark, and bring him with thee; for he is profitable to me for the ministry. This appears also from <reference osisRef="Plm.1.24">Plm 1:24</reference>, where Mark is styled Paul's fellow-laborer; and from <reference osisRef="Col.4.10">Col 4:10</reference>, where we find the apostle recommending him in a particular manner to the Church of God at that place. He is generally supposed to have been particularly intimate with St. Peter, to have written his Gospel at Rome, a.d. 64, and to have died at Alexandria in Egypt, in the eighth year of the reign of Nero. Dr. Lardner has fully proved that Mark the evangelist, and John Mark nephew to Barnabas, were one and the same person. See his Works, vol. vi. p. 77, etc. <div eID="gen39046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39047" type="x-p"/> How Mark composed his Gospel, is a question not yet decided among learned men. Many of the primitive fathers, such as Papias, Clemens, Alexandrinus, Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Eusebius, etc., believed that he was only the amanuensis of St. Peter; that this apostle, through modesty, would not put his name to the work, but dictated the whole account, and Mark wrote it down from his mouth. St. Augustine appears to have been the first who maintained that Mark abridged St. Matthew's Gospel; and that it is not to be considered as an original work: - on this opinion several remarks will be made in the course of these notes. Others suppose that Mark compiled it, partly out of Matthew's Gospel, and partly out of the Gospel of Luke. But most of these are conjectures which appear to have very little foundation. Critics are also divided concerning the language in which it was written, and the people to whom it was sent. Some have contended for a Latin original, because of several Latin words found in it, such as σπεκουλατωρ, <reference osisRef="Mar.6.27">Mar 6:27</reference>, one of the guard; κεντυριων, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.39">Mar 15:39</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.44">Mar 15:44</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.15.46">Mar 15:46</reference>, a centurion, a captain of one hundred men; συσσημον, <reference osisRef="Mar.14.44">Mar 14:44</reference>, a signal, a sign agreed on. But such words are better accounted for by supposing that his Gospel was written for the use of the Roman people; and that it is on this account that he wholly passes by the genealogy of our Lord, as being a point of no consequence to Gentile converts, though very necessary for the Jews, and especially the Jews of Palestine. That it was originally written in Greek, is a point now acknowledged by almost all learned men. <div eID="gen39047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39048" type="x-p"/> It may be necessary to state the things omitted by Mark in the beginning of his Gospel which are mentioned by Matthew and Luke. <div eID="gen39048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39049" type="x-p"/> 1. The Preface, found in Luke and John, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.1">Luk 1:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Joh.1.1">Joh 1:1</reference>. <div eID="gen39049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39050" type="x-p"/> 2. The Conception of Elizabeth, Luke 1:5-25. <div eID="gen39050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39051" type="x-p"/> 3. The Salutation of Mary, <reference osisRef="Luk.1.26-Luk.1.38">Luk 1:26-38</reference>. <div eID="gen39051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39052" type="x-p"/> 4. Mary's Visit to Elizabeth, Luke 1:39-56. <div eID="gen39052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39053" type="x-p"/> 5. John Baptist's Birth, Luke 1:57-79. <div eID="gen39053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39054" type="x-p"/> 6. The Angel's Appearance to Joseph, <reference osisRef="Mat.1.18-Mat.1.25">Mat 1:18-25</reference>. <div eID="gen39054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39055" type="x-p"/> 7. The Birth of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.1.25">Mat 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.2.1-Luk.2.7">Luk 2:1-7</reference>. <div eID="gen39055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39056" type="x-p"/> 8. The Genealogy of Christ, Matthew 1:1-17; Luke 3:23-38. <div eID="gen39056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39057" type="x-p"/> 9. The Appearance of the Angel to the Shepherds, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.8-Luk.2.20">Luk 2:8-20</reference>. <div eID="gen39057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39058" type="x-p"/> 10. The Circumcision of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mat.1.25">Mat 1:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.2.21">Luk 2:21</reference>. <div eID="gen39058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39059" type="x-p"/> 11. The Presentation of Christ in the Temple, Luke 2:22-38. <div eID="gen39059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39060" type="x-p"/> 12. The Coming of the Magi, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.1-Mat.2.12">Mat 2:1-12</reference>. <div eID="gen39060" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39061" type="x-p"/> 13. The Flight into Egypt, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.13-Mat.2.15">Mat 2:13-15</reference>. <div eID="gen39061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39062" type="x-p"/> 14. Herod's Murder of the Innocents, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.16-Mat.2.18">Mat 2:16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen39062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39063" type="x-p"/> 15. The Return of the Holy Family from Egypt, <reference osisRef="Mat.2.19-Mat.2.23">Mat 2:19-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.2.39">Luk 2:39</reference>. <div eID="gen39063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39064" type="x-p"/> 16. Christ's Journey to Jerusalem when twelve years of age, <reference osisRef="Luk.2.40-Luk.2.48">Luk 2:40-48</reference>. <div eID="gen39064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39065" type="x-p"/> From the particulars enumerated here, it appears that the things omitted by Mark are also omitted by John, except the Preface; and that St. Luke is the most circumstantial. <div eID="gen39065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39066" type="x-p"/> For other particulars relative to this Gospel, see at the end of the last chapter. <div eID="gen39066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39067" type="x-p"/> The mission, preaching, and success of John Baptist, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.1-Mar.1.5">Mar 1:1-5</reference>. His manner of life, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.6">Mar 1:6</reference>. Proclaims Christ, and baptizes him in Jordan, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.7-Mar.1.11">Mar 1:7-11</reference>. The temptation of Christ, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.12">Mar 1:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.13">Mar 1:13</reference>. John being put in prison, Christ begins to preach, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.14">Mar 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.15">Mar 1:15</reference>. He calls Andrew and Simon, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.16-Mar.1.18">Mar 1:16-18</reference>. James and John, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.19">Mar 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.20">Mar 1:20</reference>. Teaches in Capernaum, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.21">Mar 1:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.22">Mar 1:22</reference>. Casts out a demon, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.23-Mar.1.28">Mar 1:23-28</reference>. Goes into the house of Simon, and heals his mother-in-law, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.29-Mar.1.31">Mar 1:29-31</reference>. Heals many diseased persons, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.32-Mar.1.34">Mar 1:32-34</reference>. Goes to the desert, and is followed by his disciples, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.35-Mar.1.37">Mar 1:35-37</reference>. Preaches in different towns and synagogues of Galilee, and casts out devils, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.38">Mar 1:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.39">Mar 1:39</reference>. Cleanses a leper, who publishes abroad his miraculous cure, <reference osisRef="Mar.1.40-Mar.1.45">Mar 1:40-45</reference>. <div eID="gen39067" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39068" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen39068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39069" type="x-p"/> The beginning of the Gospel - It is with the utmost propriety that Mark begins the Gospel dispensation by the preaching of John the Baptist, he being the forerunner of Jesus Christ, and the first proclaimer of the incarnated Messiah. Gospel - for the meaning of the word see the preface to Matthew. <div eID="gen39069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39070" type="x-p"/> Son of God - To point out his Divine origin; and thus glancing at his miraculous conception. This was an essential character of the Messiah. See <reference osisRef="Mat.16.16">Mat 16:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mat.26.63">Mat 26:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luk.22.67">Luk 22:67</reference>, etc.
entries.80a17d0988fb60205eae41f039144c78077450e3: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen39070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39071" type="x-p"/> As it is written in the prophets - Rather, As it is written by Isaiah the prophet. I think this reading should be adopted, instead of that in the common text. It is the reading of the Codex Bezae, Vatican, and several other MSS. of great repute. It is found also in the Syriac, Persic, Coptic, Armenian, Gothic, Vulgate, and Itala versions, and in several of the fathers. As this prophecy is found both in Isaiah and Malachi, probably the reading was changed to τοις προφηταις, the prophets, that it might comprehend both. In one of Asseman's Syriac copies, both Isaiah and Malachi are mentioned. See all the authorities in Griesbach, 2d edit.; and see the parallel place in Matthew, <reference osisRef="Mat.3.3">Mat 3:3</reference>, where the Prophet Isaiah is mentioned, which seems fully to establish the authority of this reading.
entries.e98a61fa1deeef4996441c702923dcce519a06dd: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen39071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39072" type="x-p"/> The voice of one crying - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.1-Mat.3.3">Mat 3:1-3</reference> (note).
entries.40740a39dd4cc2dcf4ea01a038a61c26015bd8ef: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen39072" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39073" type="x-p"/> John - The original name is nearly lost in the Greek Ιωαννης, and in the Latin Johannes, and almost totally so in the English John. The original name is יהוחנן Yehochanan, compounded of יהוה חנן Yehovah chanan, the grace or mercy of Jehovah: a most proper and significant name for the forerunner of the God of All Grace. It was John's business to proclaim the Gospel of the grace of God, and to point out that Lamb or sacrifice of God which takes away the sin of the world. <div eID="gen39073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39074" type="x-p"/> For the remission of sins - Or, toward the remission - εις αφεσιν. They were to repent, and be baptized in reference to the remission of sins. Repentance prepared the soul for it, and Baptism was the type or pledge of it. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.2">Mat 3:2</reference> (note).
entries.977a36cd28144a32474375cc5f44a29457f03bfe: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen39074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39075" type="x-p"/> All the land - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.4-Mat.3.6">Mat 3:4-6</reference> (note). <div eID="gen39075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39076" type="x-p"/> Confessing their sins - It was an invariable custom among the Jews to admit no proselyte to baptism, till he had, in the most solemn manner, declared that he forever had renounced all idolatrous worship, all heathenish superstitions, and promised an entire and unreserved submission to the law of Moses. This was necessary for a proselyte adult - a child dedicated to God by baptism must be brought up in this faith.
entries.f3a3422009337c449fee2b8ce3e8370547a479f9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen39076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39077" type="x-p"/> John was clothed, etc. - See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.4">Mat 3:4</reference>.
entries.c3d521a14282f667d15ac596fec938c015336458: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen39077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39078" type="x-p"/> The latchet of whose shoes - The shoe of the ancients was properly only a sole tied round the foot and ankle with strings or thongs. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.11">Mat 3:11</reference> (note).
entries.8bb44ea1958b789451bb73e24a5507cf8ddf5196: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen39078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39079" type="x-p"/> I indeed have baptized you with water - As if he had said: This baptism is not to be rested in; it is only an emblem of that which you must receive from him who is mightier than I. It is he only who can communicate the Holy Spirit; and water baptism is nothing, but as it points out, and leads to, the baptism of the Holy Ghost. The subject of these two verses is not found in Matthew nor John; but is mentioned with some varying circumstances by Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.3.16">Luk 3:16</reference>.
entries.e06157f9f299c64b01f93f5ebd10f2d4a9bc912b: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen39079" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39080" type="x-p"/> See the subject of these verses which contain the account of our Lord's baptism, explained. <reference osisRef="Mat.3.13-Mat.3.17">Mat 3:13-17</reference> (note).
entries.929bc62a331564009a1806ab88f8e56621656882: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen39080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39081" type="x-p"/> The Spirit driveth him - Εκβαλλει, putteth him forth. St. Matthew says, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.1">Mat 4:1</reference>, ανηχθη, was brought up. See this important subject of our Lord's temptation explained at large, <reference osisRef="Mat.4.1-Mat.4.11">Mat 4:1-11</reference> (note).
entries.ab9d5a05fe17470bc0a0b7f00179a50cbe90cbfe: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen39081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39082" type="x-p"/> With the wild beasts - This is a curious circumstance, which is mentioned by none of the other evangelists; and seems to intimate that he was in the most remote, unfrequented, and savage part of the desert; which, together with the diabolic influence, tended to render the whole scene the more horrid. Perhaps this very circumstance is mentioned, as emblematical of that savage and brutal cruelty with which he was persecuted to death by the Jews and Gentiles, instigated thereto by the malice of Satan.
entries.2a1bd8bca31cf609220ae055b34b9754744cf13d: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen39082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39083" type="x-p"/> Preaching the Gospel of the kingdom - See the notes on <reference osisRef="Mat.3.2">Mat 3:2</reference>; and on the office of the preacher, or herald, at the end of that chapter.
entries.ccee173af690ea1eb2d762792fbd7af48d52402b: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen39083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39084" type="x-p"/> The time is fulfilled - That is, the time appointed for sending the Messiah; and particularly the time specified by Daniel, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24-Dan.9.27">Dan 9:24-27</reference>. Here are four points worthy of deep attention, in the preaching of the Son of God. <div eID="gen39084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39085" type="x-p"/> 1. Every thing that is done is according to a plan laid by the Divine wisdom, and never performed till the time appointed was filled up. <div eID="gen39085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39086" type="x-p"/> 2. That the kingdom and reign of sin are to be destroyed, and the kingdom of grace and heaven established in their place. <div eID="gen39086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39087" type="x-p"/> 3. That the kingdom of God, and his reign by grace, begins with repentance for past sins. <div eID="gen39087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39088" type="x-p"/> 4. That this reign of grace is at hand; and that nothing but an obstinate perseverance in sin and impenitence can keep any soul out of it; and that now is the accepted time to enter in.
entries.ceff8ca970531d12780087d6784ed636e8b63ee1: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen39088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39089" type="x-p"/> As he walked by the sea, etc. - See on <reference osisRef="Mat.4.18-Mat.4.22">Mat 4:18-22</reference> (note). <div eID="gen39089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39090" type="x-p"/> Andrew his brother - Instead of the common reading, αδελφον αυτου, his brother, the best MSS. and versions have αδελφου του Σιμωνος, the brother of Simon, which should be received into the text. The most eminent critics approve of this reading.
entries.f53a6f7c501397894a15c2b41dddb648287e1807: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen39090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39091" type="x-p"/> Capernaum - See <reference osisRef="Mat.4.13">Mat 4:13</reference>. <div eID="gen39091" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39092" type="x-p"/> He entered into the synagogue - Their synagogues - εν ταις συναγωγαις αυτων, according to the Syriac, which has the word in the plural.
entries.148492ac93e564c935ca6e2119ca47529cad7192: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen39092" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39093" type="x-p"/> As one that had authority - From God, to do what he was doing; and to teach a pure and beneficent system of truth. <div eID="gen39093" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39094" type="x-p"/> And not as the scribes - Who had no such authority, and whose teaching was not accompanied by the power of God to the souls of the people: <div eID="gen39094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39095" type="x-p"/> 1. because the matter of the teaching did not come from God; and <div eID="gen39095" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39096" type="x-p"/> 2. because the teachers themselves were not commissioned by the Most High. See the note on <reference osisRef="Mat.7.28">Mat 7:28</reference>.
entries.c1fd4cffaad4cf774a41ec1ccf8b7db432e00353: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen39096" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39097" type="x-p"/> A man with an unclean spirit - This demoniac is only mentioned by Mark and Luke, <reference osisRef="Luk.4.33">Luk 4:33</reference>. It seems the man had lucid intervals; else he could not have been admitted into the synagogue. Unclean or impure spirit - a common epithet for those fallen spirits: but here it may mean, one who filled the heart of him he possessed with Lascivious thoughts, images, desires, and propensities. By giving way to the first attacks of such a spirit, he may soon get in, and take full possession of the whole soul.
entries.7a594eb7ea09fcaeeaef9fbd78663b3049545072: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen39097" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39098" type="x-p"/> What have we to do with thee - Or, What is it to us and to thee? or, What business hast thou with us? That this is the meaning of the original, τι ἡμιν και σοι, Kypke has sufficiently shown. There is a phrase exactly like it in <reference osisRef="2Sam.16.10">2Sam 16:10</reference>. What have I to do with you, ye sons of Zeruiah? מה לי ולכם בני צרויה ma li v'lacem beney Tseruiah, What business have ye with me, or, Why do ye trouble me, ye sons of Tseruiah? The Septuagint translate the Hebrew just as the evangelist does here, τι εμοι και ὑμιν; it is the same idiom in both places, as there can be no doubt that the demoniac spoke in Hebrew, or in the Chaldeo-Syriac dialect of that language, which was then common in Judea. See on <reference osisRef="Mat.8.29">Mat 8:29</reference> (note). <div eID="gen39098" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39099" type="x-p"/> Art thou come to destroy us? - We may suppose this spirit to have felt and spoken thus: "Is this the time of which it hath been predicted, that in it the Messiah should destroy all that power which we have usurped and exercised over the bodies and souls of men? Alas! it is so. I now plainly see who thou art - the Holy One of God, who art come to destroy unholiness, in which we have our residence, and through which we have our reign in the souls of men." An unholy spirit is the only place where Satan can have his full operation, and show forth the plenitude of his destroying power.
entries.588c91055fe4c6b2471c96f8751ddd1dd62e362f: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen39099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39100" type="x-p"/> And Jesus rebuked him - A spirit of this cast will only yield to the sovereign power of the Son of God. All watchings, fasting, and mortifications, considered in themselves, will do little or no good. Uncleanness, of every description, will only yield to the rebuke of God.
entries.22776ea3df5e6b78de08871743ceb54d066d5a02: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen39100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39101" type="x-p"/> And when the unclean spirit had torn him - And had thrown him down in the midst, <reference osisRef="Luk.4.35">Luk 4:35</reference>, και σπαραξαν, and convulsed him. Never was there a person possessed by an unclean spirit who did not suffer a convulsion, perhaps a total ruin of nature by it. Sins of uncleanness, as the apostle intimates, are against the body; they sap the foundation of life, so that there are very few of this class, whether male or female, that live out half their days: they generally die martyrs to their lusts. When the propensities of the flesh are most violent in a person who is determined to serve God, it is often a proof that these are the last efforts of the impure spirit, who has great rages because he knows his time is but short.
entries.f4b8d57f8d6fa198da1a7c96d5162306c85d6411: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen39101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39102" type="x-p"/> What thing is this? - Words of surprise and astonishment. <div eID="gen39102" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39103" type="x-p"/> And what new doctrine - I have added the particle and, from the Syriac, as it helps the better to distinguish the members of the sentence; but there is a vast diversity in the MSS. on this verse. See Griesbach. <div eID="gen39103" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39104" type="x-p"/> For with authority - They had never heard such a gracious doctrine, and never saw any teaching supported by miracles before. How much must this person be superior to men! - they are brought into subjection by unclean spirits; this person subjects unclean spirits to himself.
entries.a3122d78adce2128eaec168e63abd5bf9f01ea48: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen39104" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39105" type="x-p"/> And immediately his fame spread abroad - The miracle which he had performed was - <div eID="gen39105" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39106" type="x-p"/> 1. great; <div eID="gen39106" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39107" type="x-p"/> 2. evidenced much benevolence in the worker of it; and <div eID="gen39107" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39108" type="x-p"/> 3. was very public, being wrought in the synagogue. <div eID="gen39108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39109" type="x-p"/> The many who saw it published it wherever they went; and thus the fame of Christ, as an incomparable teacher, and unparalleled worker of miracles, became soon spread abroad through the land. <div eID="gen39109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39110" type="x-p"/> The word, ευθεως, immediately, occurs more frequently in this evangelist than in any other writer of the new covenant: it is very often superfluous, and may often be omitted in the translation, without any prejudice to the sense of the passage in which it is found. It seems to be used by St. Mark, as our ancient writers used forsooth, and such like words.

entries.e758c752595ab564ddcb00ee90b05af98f525fdb: <hi type="bold">Verse 38</hi> <div eID="gen39117" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39118" type="x-p"/> The next towns - Κωμοπολεις properly signifies such towns as resembled cities for magnitude and number of inhabitants, but which were not walled as were cities. entries.54698dd37382893ef562238ae36e6b408045b505: <hi type="bold">Verse 39</hi> <div eID="gen39119" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39120" type="x-p"/> And he preached - He continued preaching - Ην κηρυσσων: this is the proper meaning of the words: he never slackened his pace - he continued proclaiming the glad tidings of salvation to all - there was no time to be lost - immortal souls were perishing for lack of knowledge; and the grand adversary was prowling about, seeking whom he might devour. entries.4e837c28806b46fc2a8edd8752f9526054ee0bb6: <hi type="bold">Verse 45</hi> <div eID="gen39134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39135" type="x-p"/> Began to publish it much - Began to publish πολλα, many things; probably all that he had heard about our Lord's miraculous works. <div eID="gen39135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39136" type="x-p"/> And to blaze abroad the matter - That is, his own healing; thinking he could never speak too much, nor too well, of him who had thus mercifully and miraculously cleansed him. <div eID="gen39136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39137" type="x-p"/> Jesus could no more openly enter into the city - A city of Galilee, probably Chorazin or Bethsaida, in which he did not appear, for fear of exciting the jealousy of the secular government, or the envy and malice of the Jewish rulers. <div eID="gen39137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen39138" type="x-p"/> And they came to him from every quarter - So generally had the poor man, who was cleansed of his leprosy, spread abroad his fame. And can we suppose that, of all these people who came to him from all parts, and to whom he preached the glad tidings of the kingdom, by the power and authority of God, few or none were saved? This is a common opinion; but every person who seriously considers it must see that it is unfounded. Without doubt, Christ had thousands that were brought to God by his ministry; though, in general, only those are mentioned who were constant attendants on his person. It would be strange, if, while God manifested in the flesh was preacher, there should be few brought to the knowledge of themselves, and of the truth! In this respect he does not permit his faithful ministers to labor in vain. The Son of man sowed the seed of the kingdom; and it afterwards produced a plentiful harvest. Multitudes of Jews were converted by the preaching of the Gospel; and the first Christian Church was founded at Jerusalem.  <chapter eID="Mark.1"/> <div eID="gen39138" type="x-p"/>

Verse 66. Sealing the stone. The sepulchre was made sure, by affixing the large stone to the entrance in such a way that it could not be removed without detection. It was sealed. In what way this was done cannot now be certainly told. The cave in which Daniel was cast was fastened in the same manner, and sealed with the king's signet, (Dan 6:17) perhaps by fastening the stone in its place with cords, and bringing them together and uniting them with wax, and impressing on that the seal of the king. In this way letters and books were anciently sealed. Possibly on the sepulchre of Jesus was impressed in this manner the seal of Pilate--the seal of office-- making it doubly sure. Or it may be, that the stone was fitted into the tomb with clay or cement, and on that was impressed the seal of Pilate.

Setting a watch. That is, as large a number of soldiers as they judged necessary to secure the tomb.

We cannot but be struck with the wisdom of God, in ordering the circumstances of the Saviour's burial in such a manner as to avoid the possibility of deception. Had all this been done by his friends, it might have been said that they only pretended to secure the tomb, and only pretended that he was dead. But he was adjudged to be dead by the Jews themselves; Pilate was satisfied that that was the fact they had their own way about his burial; he was buried alone; the place of his sepulchre was made sure--expressly to prevent his being removed; and they placed around him a guard, in their own judgment, large enough to prevent his being taken away by force or strength. His very enemies, therefore, took every possible precaution to place his resurrection beyond the possibility of suspicion of fraud and imposture, and were the very means of furnishing the most striking proof that his death, burial, and resurrection were not impositions, but most affecting, awful, and yet cheering realities.

entries.4ad1c81fc2688efcfbdf2e52ad04d69992b2a494:
THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MARK

PREFACE

Of Mark, the writer of this gospel, little is certainly known. He is commonly supposed to be the same that is several times mentioned in the New Testament. He was not an apostle, or companion of the Lord Jesus, during his ministry, though some of the Fathers affirm that he was one of the seventy disciples. This is improbable, as he is mentioned by Peter (1Pet 5:13) as his son; from which it is supposed that he was converted by the instrumentality of Peter.

From the New Testament, we learn that he was sister's son to Barnabas, (Col 4:10;) and that his mother's name was Mary, a pious woman in Jerusalem, at whose house the apostles and primitive Christians often assembled, Acts 12:12.

His Hebrew name was John, (Acts 12:12,) and it is probable that he adopted a name better known, or more familiar, when he visited the Gentiles, a practice not uncommon in that age. He was at first the companion of Paul and Barnabas, in their journeys to propagate Christianity, Acts 13:5. He chose not to attend them through their whole journey, but left them in Pamphylia, and probably returned to Jerusalem, Acts 15:38. Probably at this time he was the companion of Peter, and travelled with him to Babylon, 1Pet 5:13. Afterwards he went with Barnabas to Cyprus, Acts 15:39. Subsequently he went to Rome, at the express desire of Paul, in company with Timothy, 2Ti 4:11. He remained at Rome while Paul was a captive there, but how long is uncertain, Col 4:10; Phm 1:24. From Eusebius, Epiphanius, and Jerome, we hear that Mark went from Rome to Alexandria, in Egypt, where he planted a church, and died and was buried in the eighth year of the reign of Nero, A.D. 64.

The time when this gospel was written is not certainly known. It is supposed to have been between the years 56 and 63. It is allowed by all that it was written at Rome; of course, it was during the latter years of his life, after the apostles had left Judea, Mk 16:20. Mark was, for a considerable time, the companion of Peter. Though he had not himself been with the Saviour in his ministry, yet, from his long acquaintance with Peter, he was familiar with the events of his life, and with his instructions. The uniform testimony of the Fathers is, that he was the interpreter of Peter, and that he wrote this Gospel under the eye of Peter, and with his approbation. It has come down to us, therefore, with the sanction of Peter's authority. Its right to a place among the inspired books has never been questioned. That it was written by Mark; that it was with Peter's approbation; that it was a record of the facts which Peter stated in his ministry; and that it was, therefore, an inspired book has never been questioned.

MARK CHAPTER 1

Verse 1. The beginning of the Gospel. The word gospel literally signifies good tidings, and particularly the good tidings respecting the way of salvation by the Lord Jesus Christ. Some have understood the word gospel here to mean, history or life--the beginning of the history, etc. But Mark says nothing of the early life of the Saviour. It has reference rather to the preaching of John, an account of which immediately follows, and means the beginning of the good news, or annunciation, respecting the Messiah. It was very customary thus to prefix a title to a book.

The Son of God. This title was used here to attract attention, and secure the respect of those who should read this gospel. It is no common history. It does not recount the deeds of man--of a hero, or philosopher-- but the doctrines and doings of THE SON OF GOD. The history, therefore, commands respect.

Verses 12,13. Mark here relates concisely what Matthew has recorded, more at length in Mt 4.

The spirit driveth. The word driveth does not mean that he was compelled forcibly against his will to go there, but that he was inclined to go there by the Spirit, or was led there. The Spirit of God, for important purposes, caused him to go. Comp. Mt 9:25, where the same word is used in the original: "But when the people were put forth"-- in Greek, all driven out.

And was with the wild beasts. This is added to show the desolation and danger of his dwelling there. In this place, surrounded by such dangers, the temptations offered by Satan were the stronger. Amidst want, and perils, Satan might suppose he would be more easily seduced from God. But he trusted in his Father, and was alike delivered from dangers, from the wild beasts, and from the power of temptation: thus teaching us what to do in the day of danger and trial.

And the angels ministered unto him. From Lk 4:2, we learn that in those days he did eat nothing. When Mark says, therefore, that the angels ministered to him, it means after the days of temptation had expired, as is said by Matthew, Mt 4:11.

Jesus came into Galilee. He left Judea, and went into the more retired country of Galilee. He supposed that if he remained in Judea, Herod would also persecute him, and attempt his life. His time of death had not come; and he therefore prudently sought safety in retirement, hence we may learn, that when we have great duties to perform for the church of God, we are not wantonly to endanger our lives. Verse 24. Let us alone. Though but one impure spirit is mentioned as possessing this man, yet that spirit speaks also in the name of others. They were leagued together in the work of evil, and this one knew that if he was punished, others would also share the same fate.

What have we to do with thee? This seems to mean, "Have we injured thee?" or, We have done nothing to injure thee. See "1Ki 17:18". By this the spirit meant to say, that if Jesus cast him out, he would use an improper interference. But this was untrue. The possession of the man was a direct assault on God and his works. Jesus came to destroy the works of the devil, and he had a right, therefore, to liberate the captive, and to punish him who had possessed him. So Satan still considers it an infringement of his rights, when God frees a sinner from bondage, and destroys his influence over the soul. So he still pleads to be let alone, and to be suffered to lead men captive at his will.

Art thou come to destroy us? Implying that this could not be the intention of the benevolent Messiah; that to be cast out of that man would, in fact, be his destruction, and that therefore he might be suffered still to remain. Or implying, as in Mt 8:29, that the time of their destruction had not come, and that he ought not to destroy them before that.

I know thee, etc. Evil spirits seem to have been acquainted at once with the Messiah. Besides, they had learned from his miracles that he was the Messiah, and had power over them.

The Holy One of God. The Messiah. See Dan 9:24. He is called the Holy One of God, because,

1st, he was eminently pure;

2nd, because he was the only begotten Son of God--equal with the Father; and,

3rd, because he was anointed, or set apart to the work of the Messiah, the Mediator between God and man.
entries.2b2d3ff30216ce567978365ee8d7b3c4b5b58f3c:
Verse 25. And Jesus rebuked him. Chode him, or commanded him, with a threatening, to be still. This was not the man that he rebuked, but the spirit, for he instantly commanded the same being to come out of the man. In all this Jesus did not once address the man. His conversation was with evil spirit; proving conclusively that it was not a mere disease, or derangement---for how could the Son of God hold converse with disease, or delirium?--but that he conversed with a being, who also conversed, reasoned, cavilled, felt, resisted, and knew him. There are, therefore, evil spirits; and those spirits have taken possession of men.

Hold thy peace. Greek, Be muzzled. Restrain thyself. Cease from complaints, and come out of the man. This was a very signal proof of the power of Jesus, to be able by a word to silence an evil angel, and, against his will, to compel him to leave a man whom he delighted to torment.
entries.cc2d926d7e6a478e8ab48ba73f1fd101a50aaf6e: Verse 26. And when the unclean spirit, etc. Still malignant, though doomed to obey--submitting because he was obliged to, not because he chose--he exerted his last power, inflicted all the pain he could, and then bowed to the Son of God, and came out. This is the nature of an evil disposition. Though compelled to obey, though prevented by the command and Providence of God from doing what it would, yet, in seeming to obey, it does all the ill it can, and makes even the appearance of obedience the occasion for increased crime and mischief.

entries.2e98f217455c309a761d5993a30e58568fde2946:
Verses 35-37. And in the morning, rising up a great while before day. Luke says, (Lk 4:42,) it was day. The passage in Mark means, in the original, not literally a great while before day, but very early, or while there was yet much appearance of night. The place in Luke means, at daybreak, at the beginning of day. Then, also, there is much appearance of night; and Luke and Mark, therefore, refer to the same time--before it was fully light, or just at daybreak.

And departed into a solitary place, and there prayed. Here observe,

(1.) that the Saviour, though perfectly holy, regarded the duty of secret prayer as of great importance.

(2.) That he sought a solitary place for it--far away from the world, and even his disciples.

(3.) That it was early in the morning--the first thing after rising-- always the best time, and a time when it should not be omitted.

(4.) If Jesus prayed, how much more important is it for us! If he did it in the morning, how much more important is it for us, before the world gets possession of our thoughts; before Satan fills us with unholy feelings; when we rise fresh from beds of repose, and while the world around us is still! David also thus prayed, Ps 5:3. He that wishes to enjoy religion will seek a place of secret prayer in the morning. If that is omitted, all will go wrong. Our piety will wither. The world will fill our thoughts. Temptations will be strong. And through the day we shall find it impossible to raise our feelings to a state of proper devotion. This will be found to be true, universally, that the religious enjoyment through the day will be according to the state of the heart in the morning; and can, therefore be measured by our faithfulness in early secret prayer, how different, too, was the conduct of the Saviour from those who spend the precious hours of the morning in sleep! He knew the value of the morning hours; he rose while the world was still; he saw when the light spread abroad in the east with fresh tokens of his Father's presence, and joined with the universal creation in offering praise to the everywhere present God.
