entries.008449b4219f9017ef84b7c934e85f5b94e021da: Verse 37. All men seek for thee. That is, many men, or multitudes. The inquiry after him was general. They told him this evidently with a view to induce him to leave his place of retirement, and to prevail upon him to appear publicly, to instruct the multitudes.
entries.b4c570779ea445c44e8a479aabf1bf34ce4bdb1f:
Verse 38. And he said unto them, etc. This was said in answer to their implied request, that he would go and meet the multitudes. "Since the anxiety to hear the truth is so great; since such multitudes are waiting to hear the word, let us go into the next towns," etc.

Next towns. Towns in the neighbourhood or vicinity of Capernaum. He proposed to carry the gospel to them, rather than that multitudes should leave their homes and attend him in his ministry.

Towns. The word here rendered towns denotes places in size between cities and villages, or large places, but without walls.

For therefore came I forth. That is, came forth from God, or was sent by God. Luke says, (Lk 4:43) "for therefore am I sent." Compare Jn 16:28. "I came forth from the Father, and am come into the world." The meaning of this verse therefore is--Since multitudes press to hear the word, let us not remain here, but go into the neighbouring towns also, for I was sent by God not to preach at Capernaum only, but throughout Judea, and it is therefore improper to confine my labours to this place.

(x) "therefore" Isa 61:1,2, Jn 17:8
entries.73977b2a8e4bcadf117858e038d705bfaeec755d:
Verse 39. And he preached in their synagogues. See Mt 4:23.

All Galilee. See Mt 2:22.

And cast out devils. Mt 8:1-4.
entries.881acf30a753cfb9ad00122c8fc426d41932673f:
Verses 40-45. And there came a leper, etc. Mt 8:1, and Mt 8:1.

Kneeling down to him. He kneeled, and inclined his face to the ground, in token of deep humiliation, and earnest entreaty. Compare Lk 5:12.

If thou wilt. There was an acknowledgment of the almighty power of Jesus, and an appeal to his benevolence.

Make me clean. Canst heal me of this loathsome and offensive disease--in the eye of the law justly regarded as unclean--and render me legally clean, and restore me to the privileges of the congregation.

And Jesus--touched him. It was by the law considered as unclean to touch a leprous man. See Nu 5:2. The fact that Jesus touched him was evidence that the requisite power had been already put forth to heal him; that Jesus regarded him as already clean.

I will. Here was a most manifest proof of his Divine power. None but God can work a miracle. Yet Jesus does it by his own will --by an exertion of his own power. He was, therefore, Divine.

See thou say nothing to any man. The law of Moses required that the man who was healed of the leprosy should be pronounced clean by the priest, before he could be admitted again to the privileges of the congregation, Lev 19:1, etc. Christ, though he had cleansed him, yet required him to be obedient to the law of the land; to go at once to the priest, and not to make delay by stopping to converse about his being healed. It was also possible, that if he did not go at once, evil-minded men would go before him and prejudice the priest, and prevent his declaring the healing to be thorough because it was done by Jesus. It was further of importance that the priest should pronounce it to be a genuine cure, that there might be no cavils among the Jews against its being a real miracle.

Offer--those things, etc. Two birds, and cedar-wood, and scarlet, and hyssop. And after eight days, two he-lambs, without blemish, and one ewe-lamb, and fine flour, and oil, Lev 14:4,10.

For a testimony unto them. Not to the priest, but to the people, that they may have evidence that it is a real cure. The testimony of the priest on the subject would be decisive.

(a) "those things" Lev 14:2-32 (b) "testimony" Rom 15:4, 1Cor 10:11
entries.a8dd8fe599fc23d239ec59ac5b7202e3abd73a65:
Verse 45. Began to publish it much. That is, the subject of his own cure. He was so deeply affected with it, and so much rejoiced, that he followed the natural dictates of his own feelings, rather than the command of the Saviour.

Jesus could no more openly enter into the city. The word could, here, does not refer to any natural inability, or to any physical obstacle in his way, but only denotes that there was difficulty, or inconvenience, or impropriety, in his doing it then; that he judged it best not then to enter into the city. The difficulty was, probably, that his being in the city drew such crowds of people as rendered it difficult to accommodate them, or so as to excite the opposition of civil rulers.

The city. The city, or large town, where the leper was cured. The same reason for not entering that city applied also to others; so that he remained in the deserts, where the multitudes could come to him without any difficulty or opposition.

(c) "began to publish" Ps 77:11,12, Tit 1:10 (c) "and they came to him" Mk 2:13

entries.906cfefc2fc910dc1595961024bb3cbe822da5a4: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.1" sID="gen96598" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.1">Mark 1:1</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">The beginning of the Gospel.</hi> Though what we have hitherto taken out of Matthew and Luke is a part of <hi type="italic">the Gospel, </hi>yet it is not without reason that Mark makes <hi type="italic">the beginning of the Gospel </hi>to be the preaching of John the Baptist. For the Law and the Prophets then came to an end, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.17">John 1:17</reference>.) “<hi type="italic">The Law and the Prophets were until John: since that time the kingdom of God is preached</hi>,” <hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.16.16">Luke 16:16</reference><hi type="bold">.)</hi> And with this agrees most fully the quotation which he makes from the Prophet Malachi, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.1">3:1</reference>.) In order to inflame the minds of his people with a stronger desire of the promised salvation, the Lord had determined to leave them, for a time, without new prophecies. We know that the last of the true and lawful prophets was Malachi.<div eID="gen96599" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96600" type="x-p"/>That the Jews, in the meantime, may not faint with hunger, he exhorts them to continue under the Law of Moses, until the promised redemption appear. He mentions <hi type="italic">the law </hi>only, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.17">John 1:17</reference>,) because the doctrine of the Prophets was not separate from the law, but was merely an appendage and fuller exposition of it, that the form of government in the Church might depend entirely on the Law. It is no new or uncommon thing in Scripture, to include the Prophets under the name of <hi type="italic">the Law: </hi>for they were all related to it as their fountain or design. The Gospel was not an inferior appendage to the Law, but a new form of instruction, by which the former was set aside.<div eID="gen96600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96601" type="x-p"/>Malachi, distinguishing the two conditions of the Church, places the one under the Law, and commences the other with the preaching of John. He unquestionably describes the Baptist, when he says, “Behold, I send my messenger,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.1">Malachi 3:1</reference>:) for, as we have already said, that passage lays down an express distinction between the Law and the new order and condition of the Church. With the same view he had said a little before, (which is quoted by Mark, [<reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.9.13">9:13</reference>;] for the passages are quite similar,) “Behold, I send you Elijah the Prophet, before the coming of the great and dreadful day of the Lord,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.4.5">Malachi 4:5</reference>.) Again,<div eID="gen96601" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96602" type="x-p"/>“Behold, I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Mal.3.1">Malachi 3:1</reference>.)<div eID="gen96602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96603" type="x-p"/>In both passages, the Lord promises a better condition of his Church than had existed under the Law, and this unquestionably points out <hi type="italic">the beginning of the Gospel</hi> But <hi type="italic">before the Lord came</hi> to restore the Church, a forerunner or herald was to come, and announce that he was at hand. Hence we infer, that the abrogation of the Law, and <hi type="italic">the beginning of the Gospel, </hi>strictly speaking, took place when John began to preach.<div eID="gen96603" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96604" type="x-p"/>The Evangelist John presents to us Christ clothed in flesh, “the Word made flesh,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.14">John 1:14</reference>;) so that his birth and the whole history of his appearance are included in the Gospel. But here Mark inquires, when the Gospel began to be published, and, therefore, properly begins with John, who was its first minister. And with this view the Heavenly Father chose that the life of his Son should be buried, as it were, in silence, until the time of the full revelation arrived. For it did not happen without the undoubted Providence of God, that the Evangelists leave out the whole period which Christ spent in private, and pass at once from his earliest infancy to his thirtieth year, when he was openly exhibited to the world, invested with his public character as a Redeemer; Luke excepted, who slightly touches one indication of his future calling, which occurred about his twelfth year, <hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.42">Luke 2:42</reference><hi type="bold">.)</hi><div eID="gen96604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96605" type="x-p"/>It had a very close connection with this object, that we should be informed, first, that Christ is a true man, (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.1.14">John 1:14</reference>,) and next, that he is “<hi type="italic">the Son of Abraham and of David</hi>,”<hi type="bold"> (</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.1.1">Matthew 1:1</reference><hi type="bold">;)</hi> as to both of which, the Lord has been pleased to give us an attestation. The other matters which we have examined, relating to <hi type="italic">“the shepherds</hi>,” <hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.8">Luke 2:8</reference><hi type="bold">,)</hi> the <hi type="italic">“Magi,”</hi> <hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.2.1">Matthew 2:1</reference><hi type="bold">,)</hi> and <hi type="italic">“Simeon,” </hi><hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.2.25">Luke 2:25</reference><hi type="bold">,)</hi> were intended to prove his Divinity. What Luke relates about John and his father Zacharias, <hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.1.5">Luke 1:5</reference><hi type="bold">,)</hi> was a sort of preparation for the Gospel.<div eID="gen96605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96606" type="x-p"/>There is no impropriety in the change of the person which is here made, in quoting the words of Malachi. According to the prophet, God says, <hi type="italic">I send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way Before Me</hi>. Mark introduces God as addressing the Son, <hi type="italic">Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, who shall prepare thy way Before Thee</hi>. But we see that Mark had no other intention, than to express more clearly the prophet’s meaning. Mark designates Christ <hi type="italic">the Son of God</hi> The other Evangelists testify that he was born of the seed of Abraham and David, and therefore was <hi type="italic">the Son of man, </hi><hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.20">Matthew 8:20</reference><hi type="bold">.)</hi> But Mark shows us, that no redemption is to be expected but from <hi type="italic">the Son of God</hi><div eID="gen96606" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96598" osisID="Mark.1.1" type="section"/>
entries.23de7e569fe638a0fa3488542ada7d371f3a9d7a: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.14" sID="gen96881" type="section"/> <div sID="gen96882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.14">Mark 1:14</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">Preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God.</hi> Matthew appears to differ a little from the other two: for, after mentioning that Jesus left his own city Nazareth, and departed to Capernaum, he says: <hi type="italic">from that time Jesus began to preach.</hi> Luke and Mark, again, relate, that he taught publicly in his own country. But the solution is easy; for the words which Matthew employs, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἀπὸ τότε</foreign>, <hi type="italic">from that time, </hi>ought to be viewed as referring, not to what immediately precedes, but to the whole course of the narrative. Christ, therefore, entered into the exercise of his office, when he arrived at Galilee. The summary of doctrine which is given by Matthew is not at all different from what, we have lately seen, was taught by John: for it consists of two parts, — <hi type="italic">repentance, </hi>and the announcement of grace and salvation. He exhorts the Jews to conversion, because <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is at hand: </hi>that is, because God undertakes to govern his people, which is true and perfect happiness. The language of Mark is a little different, <hi type="italic">The kingdom of God is at hand: repent ye, and believe the Gospel</hi> But the meaning is the same: for, having first spoken of the restoration of the kingdom of God among the Jews, he exhorts them to repentance and faith.<div eID="gen96882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96883" type="x-p"/>But it may be asked, since <hi type="italic">repentance </hi>depends on the Gospel, why does Mark separate it from the <hi type="italic">doctrine </hi>of the Gospel? Two reasons may be assigned. God sometimes invites us to repentance, when nothing more is meant, than that we ought to change our life for the better. He afterwards shows, that conversion and “newness of life” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.6.4">Romans 6:4</reference>) are the gift of God. This is intended to inform us, that not only is our duty enjoined on us, but the grace and power of obedience are, at the same time, offered. If we understand in this way the preaching of John about repentance, the meaning will be:” The Lord commands you to turn to himself; but as you cannot accomplish this by your own endeavors, he promises the Spirit of regeneration, and therefore you must receive this grace by faith.” At the same time, the faith, which he enjoins men to give to the Gospel, ought not, by any means, to be confined to the gift of renewal, but relates chiefly to the forgiveness of sins. For John connects repentance with faith, because God reconciles us to himself in such a manner, that we serve him as a Father in holiness and righteousness.<div eID="gen96883" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen96884" type="x-p"/>Besides, there is no absurdity in saying, that <hi type="italic">to believe the Gospel </hi>is the same thing as to embrace a free righteousness: for that special relation, between faith and the forgiveness of sins, is often mentioned in Scripture; as, for example, when it teaches, that we are <hi type="italic">justified by faith,</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Rom.5.1">Romans 5:1</reference>.) In which soever of these two ways you choose to explain this passage, it still remains a settled principle, that God offers to us a free salvation, in order that we may turn to him, and live to righteousness. Accordingly, when he promises to us mercy, he calls us to deny the flesh. We must observe the designation which Paul gives to the Gospel, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God: </hi>for hence we learn, that by the preaching of the Gospel <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God </hi>is set up and established among men, and that in no other way does God reign among men. Hence it is also evident, how wretched the condition of men is without the Gospel.<div eID="gen96884" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen96881" osisID="Mark.1.14" type="section"/>
entries.1645adda7b735230d56b95067a129ed330b354e0: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.22" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.22" sID="gen97000" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97001" type="x-p"/>This demoniac was probably one of that multitude, which was mentioned, a little before, by <reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.4.24">Matthew 4:24</reference>. Yet the narrative of Mark and Luke is not superfluous: for they relate some circumstances, which not only present the miracle in a more striking light, but also contain useful instruction. The devil dexterously acknowledges, that Christ is <hi type="italic">the Holy One of God, </hi>in order to insinuate into the minds of men a suspicion, that there was some secret understanding between him and Christ. By such a trick he has since endeavored to make the Gospel suspected, and, in the present day, he is continually making similar attempts. That is the reason why Christ rebukes him. It is, no doubt, possible, that this confession was violently extorted from him: but there is no inconsistency between the two suppositions, that he is forced to yield to the power of Christ, and therefore <hi type="italic">cries out</hi> that he is <hi type="italic">the Holy One of God,</hi> — and yet that he cunningly attempts to shroud in his own darkness the glory of Christ. At the same time, we must observe that, while he flatters Christ in this manner, he indirectly withdraws himself from his power, and in this way contradicts himself. For why was Christ sanctified by the Father, but that he might deliver men from the tyranny of the devil, and overturn his kingdom? But as Satan cannot endure that power, which he feels to be destructive to himself, he would desire that Christ should satisfy himself with an empty title, without exercising it on the present occasion. <note n="344"> <div sID="gen97002" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais pource que Satan ne pent endurer ceste vertue et puissance, aquelle il sait estre le destruire et ruiner, il voudroit bien que Christ se contenant d'un beau titre en l'air, se reposast, et se deportast de luy rien faire</foreign>.” — “But because Satan cannot endure that power and might, which he knows to be to destroy and ruin him, he would rather wish that Christ, satisfying himself with a fine title in the air, should take repose, and refrain from doing any thing to him.<div eID="gen97002" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen97001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen97003" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.22">Mark 1:22</reference></hi>;<hi type="bold"> <reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.4.32">Luke 4:32</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">And they were astonished at his doctrine</hi> The meaning of the Evangelists is, that the power of the Spirit shone in the preaching <note n="345"> <div sID="gen97004" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">En la facon d’enseigner de Jesus Christ</foreign>;” — “in Jesus Christ's manner of teaching.”<div eID="gen97004" type="x-p"/> </note> of Christ with such brightness, as to extort admiration even from irreligious and cold hearers. Luke says, that <hi type="italic">his discourse was accompanied with power, </hi>that is, full of majesty. Mark expresses it more fully, by adding a contrast, that it was unlike the manner of teaching of <hi type="italic">the Scribes</hi> As they were false expounders of Scripture, their doctrine was literal and dead, breathed nothing of the power of the Spirit, and was utterly destitute of majesty. The same kind of coldness may be now observed in the speculative theology of Popery. Those masters do indeed thunder out whatever they think proper in a sufficiently magisterial style; but as their manner of discoursing about divine things is so profane, that their controversies exhibit no traces of religion, what they bring forward is all affectation and mere drivelling: for the declaration of the Apostle Paul holds true, that <hi type="italic">the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power, </hi>(<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.4.20">1 Corinthians 4:20</reference>.) In short, the Evangelists mean that, while the manner of teaching, which then prevailed, was so greatly degenerated and so extremely corrupted, that it did not impress the minds of men with any reverence for God, the preaching of Christ was eminently distinguished by the divine power of the Spirit, which procured for him the respect of his hearers. This is the <hi type="italic">power, </hi>or rather the majesty and <hi type="italic">authority, </hi>at which the people were astonished.<div eID="gen97003" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.22" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97000" osisID="Mark.1.22" type="section"/>
entries.534244c0b8aada5db0e29020e5effc80cf60f057: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.26" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.26" sID="gen97007" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97008" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.26">Mark 1:26</reference></hi> <hi type="italic">When the unclean spirit had torn him</hi> Luke uses a milder phrase, <hi type="italic">when the devil had thrown him down: </hi>but they agree perfectly as to the meaning; for the design of both was to show, that the devil went out of the man in a violent manner. He threw down the unhappy man, as if he had intended to tear him: but Luke says that the attempt was unsuccessful; for <hi type="italic">he hurt him nothing</hi> Not that the attack was, in no degree whatever, attended by injury, or at least by some feeling of pain; but that the man was afterwards delivered from the devil, and restored to perfect health.<div eID="gen97008" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.26" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97007" osisID="Mark.1.26" type="section"/>
entries.273435a7dc621ddcef739148d1177caf15ec6124:
Mark 1:27 What new doctrine is this? They call it new doctrine, not by way of reproach, but as an acknowledgment, that there was something in it unusual and extraordinary. It is not for the sake of blame, or to lessen its credit, that they speak of it as new. This is rather a part of their admiration, that they pronounce it to be not common or ordinary. Their only fault lies in this, that they remain in their state of hesitation,
“En leur doute et estonnement.” — “In their doubt and astonishment.”
whereas the children of God ought to make increasing progress.
MATTHEW 8:14-18; MARK 1:29-39; LUKE 4:38-44
Matthew 8:14-18
Mark 1:29-39
Luke 4:38-44
14. And when Jesus had come into Peter’s house, he saw his mother-in-law lying in bed, and afflicted with fever. 15. And he touched her hand, and the fever left her, and she arose and waited on them. 16. And when the evening had approached, they brought to him many demoniacs, and he cast out the spirits by his word, and healed all that were diseased: 17. That it might be fulfilled which was spoken by Isaiah the prophet, when he saith, He hath taken our diseases. 18. And when Jesus had seen great multitudes around him, he commanded that they should depart to the other side.
29. And immediately going out of the synagogue, they came, with James and John, into the house of Simon and Andrew. 30. And Simon’s mother-in-law lay afflicted with fever and immediately they speak to him about her. 31. And approaching, he raised her, by taking her hand, and the fever immediately left her, and she waited on them. 32. And in the evening, when the sun had set, they brought to him all who were diseased, and who were possessed by devils. 33. And the whole city was assembled at the door. 34. And hehealed many that were ill of various diseases, and cast out many devils: and he did not permit the devils to say that they knew him. 35. And in the morning, while it was still very dark, Jesus, when he had risen, went out, and departed into a desert place, and there prayed. 36. And Simon followed him, as also those who were with him. 37. And when they had found him, they said to him, All seek thee. 38. And he saith to them, Let us go into the adjoining villages, that I preach there also: for on this account I came out. 39. And he preached in their synagogues in all Galilee, and cast out devils.
38. And when Jesus had risen out of the synagogue, he entered into Simon’s house. And Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a great fever, and they besought him for her. 39. And standing over her, he rebuked the fever, and the fever left her: and immediately rising, she waited on them. 40. And when the sun was setting, all, who had persons laboring under various diseases, brought them to him: and he, laying hands upon each, healed them. 41. And the devils went out of many, crying and saying, Thou art Christ, the Son of God. And, rebuking, he did not permit them to speak those things, that they knew that he was Christ. 42. And when it was day, going out, he went into a desert place, and multitudes sought him: and came even to him, and held him, that he might not depart from them. 43. To whom he saith, I must also preach the kingdom of God in other cities: for on this account am I sent. 44. And he preached in the synagogues of Galilee.
entries.8ec09a01e8de37e8a18199bb6f738895e7ac787e: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.29" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.29" sID="gen97023" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97024" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.29">Mark 1:29</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">They came, with James and John, into the house of Simon and Andrew.</hi> There is reason to conjecture, that Matthew does not relate this history in its proper order: for Mark expressly states, that there were only four disciples who attended Christ. Besides, when he left the synagogue, he went straight to Peter’s house; which also shows clearly, that Matthew did not observe, with exactness, the order of time. The Evangelists appear to have taken particular notice of this miracle; not that, in itself, it was more remarkable, or more worthy of being recorded, than other miracles, — but because, by means of it, Christ gave to his disciples a private and familiar illustration of his grace. Another reason was, that the healing of one woman gave occasion to many miracles, so that they came to him in great numbers, from every direction, to implore his assistance. A single word, in Luke’s narrative, presents to us more strikingly the power which Christ displayed; for he says, that <hi type="italic">Simon’s mother-in-law was held by a GREAT</hi> <hi type="italic">fever.</hi> It was a clearer and more affecting proof of divine power, that, in a moment, and by a single touch, he removed a strong and violent disease. He might have done it by the slightest expression of his will; but he <hi type="italic">touched her hand,</hi> <hi type="bold">(</hi><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.15">Matthew 8:15</reference><hi type="bold">,)</hi> either to mark his affection, or because he was aware that this sign was, at that time, advantageous: for we know, that he freely used outward signs, when the time required them.<div eID="gen97024" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.29" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97023" osisID="Mark.1.29" type="section"/>
entries.d8448e6474f983d974d73ee737c85b39789cfe04: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.34" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.34" sID="gen97030" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97031" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.34">Mark 1:34</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">He did not permit the devils to speak.</hi> There might be two reasons why <hi type="italic">he did not permit </hi>them: a general reason, because the time of the full revelation was not yet come; and a special reason, which we hinted at a little ago, that he refused to have, as heralds and witnesses of his divinity, those whose praise could have no other effect than to soil and injure his character. This latter reason is undoubtedly true: for he must have known, that the prince of death, and his agents, are in a state of irreconcileable enmity with the Author of eternal salvation and life.<div eID="gen97031" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.34" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97030" osisID="Mark.1.34" type="section"/>

Mark1:38. For on this account I came out. Luke 4:43. For on this account am I sent. These words deserve our attention: for they contain a declaration of his earnest desire to fulfill his office. But it will perhaps be asked, is it better that the ministers of the Gospel should run here and there, to give only a slight and partial taste of it in each place, or that they should remain, and instruct perfectly the hearers whom they have once obtained? I reply. The design of Christ, which is here mentioned, was agreeable to the injunction and call of the Father, and was founded on the best reasons. For it was necessary that Christ should travel, within a short period, throughout Judea, to awaken the minds of men, on all sides, as if by the sound of a trumpet, to hear the Gospel. But on this subject we must treat more fully under another passage.

entries.4410c8b9fa93f60758c3361645669637dfda0e53: <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.44" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Mark.1.44" sID="gen97773" type="section"/> <div sID="gen97774" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold"><reference osisRef="Bible:Matt.8.4">Matthew 8:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Bible:Mark.1.44">Mark 1:44</reference>.</hi> <hi type="italic">For a testimony to them</hi> Some consider <hi type="italic">testimony </hi>to mean here a law or statute, as it is said in the Book of Psalms, God laid down this <hi type="italic">“</hi>for a testimony to Israel,” (<reference osisRef="Bible:Ps.122.4">Psalm 122:4</reference>.) But this appears to me to be a poor exposition: for I have no doubt that the pronoun <hi type="italic">to them </hi>refers to the priests. <note n="496"> <div sID="gen97775" type="x-p"/> According to the view which Calvin rejects, the words, <hi type="italic">which Moses commanded for a testimony to them, </hi>mean, “which Moses delivered <hi type="italic">to them, </hi>that is, to the people of Israel, as a divine ordinance.” The view which he adopts may be more clearly brought out by a different arrangement of the words. <hi type="italic">Present, for a testimony </hi>to them, that is, “to the priests,” <hi type="italic">the offering which Moses commanded</hi>. —<hi type="italic"> Ed</hi><div eID="gen97775" type="x-p"/> </note> Christ said this, in my opinion, with a view to the present occurrence: for this miracle was afterwards to be a sufficiently clear proof for convicting them of ingratitude. There is nothing inconsistent with this in the command which Christ gave to the leper to maintain silence: for he did not intend that the remembrance of the miracle which he had wrought should remain always buried. When the leper, at the command of Christ, came into the presence of the priest, this was <hi type="italic">a testimony to them, </hi>which would render them inexcusable, if they refused to receive Christ as the minister of God; and would, at the same time, take away occasion for slander, since Christ did not neglect a single point of the law. In a word, if they were not past cure, they might be led to Christ; while, on the other hand, so solemn a testimony of God was sufficiently powerful to condemn them, if they were unbelievers.<div eID="gen97774" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Mark.1.44" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen97773" osisID="Mark.1.44" type="section"/>

Mark 1:45. So that Jesus could no longer enter openly into cities Hence we learn the reason why Christ did not wish the miracle to be so soon made known. It was that he might have more abundant opportunity and freedom for teaching. Not that his enemies rose against him, and attempted to shut his mouth, but because the common people were so eager to demand miracles, that no room was left for doctrine. He wished that they would all be more attentive to the word than to signs. Luke accordingly says, that he sought retirement in the deserts He avoided a crowd of men, because he saw, that he would not satisfy the wishes of the people, without overwhelming his doctrine by a superfluity of miracles.
“Que quant et quant il ne fist tant de miracles, que cela les empescheroit de bien penser a la doctrine;” — “without doing so many miracles as to prevent them from thinking properly about his doctrine.”

                        </ns0:gap>he Gosp<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>l, or in the Gospel,</ns0:hi> to believe the Gospel is one thing, <ns0:hi>to believe in the Gospel,</ns0:hi> (as it is here in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi>) is another.                      <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 29.</ns0:note> taught them as one that had authority, and not as the scribes.<ns0:note place="bottom">We heard before that the <ns0:hi>Synagogues</ns0:hi> were much of the Nature of our <ns0:hi>Parish Churches,</ns0:hi> places where People ordinarily met to<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gether on the <ns0:hi>Sabbath days,</ns0:hi> to Worshp God by <ns0:hi>Prayer,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>reading</ns0:hi> the <ns0:hi>Law</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Prophets,</ns0:hi> and he<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ring the Words of <ns0:hi>Exhortation,</ns0:hi> from such as the <ns0:hi>Rulers</ns0:hi> of the <ns0:hi>Synagogues</ns0:hi> appoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed thereunto. Christ ordinarily Preached in them. The <ns0:hi>Evan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gelists</ns0:hi> often mention, the Peoples admiring, being amazed, and astonished at his Doctrine, but it is one thing for People to be <ns0:hi>astonished,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>amazed,</ns0:hi> at a new Doctrine, and to admire the Preacher, another thing to <ns0:hi>believe</ns0:hi>; we read amongst the Jews, of many that were affected at the hearing of Christ, with <ns0:hi>astonish<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ment,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>admiration,</ns0:hi> but of few that believed in him, <ns0:hi>for he taught them as one that had Authority.</ns0:hi> A small derivative from this, is yet seen in the <ns0:hi>Gravity, awful presence,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Authority,</ns0:hi> (which as a great gift of God) we see still given to some faithful Ministers of Christ, such especially as God maketh a more eminent use of in the conversion of Souls. But this <ns0:hi>great Preacher</ns0:hi> had the Spirit above humane measure, <ns0:hi>not as the Scribes,</ns0:hi> the ordinary teachers of the Jews, who read their lectures of the Law, but so coldly, and without Life, and Power, as the hearts of the People were not at all affected with them, no more then with the dull telling a tale, with which neither the tellers, nor hearers were much affected.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="23">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:277" />23 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 4.33.</ns0:note> And there was in their synagogue, a man with an unclean spirit, and he cryed out,</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="24">24 Saying, Let us alone <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Matth. 8.29.</ns0:note> what have we to do with thee, thou Jesus of Nazareth, art thou come to destroy us? I know thee who thou art, the holy One of God.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> reports the same passage, he saith.—There <ns0:hi>was a Man who had the Spirit of an unclean Devil.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Devil</ns0:hi> is called an <ns0:hi>Vn<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clean Spirit,</ns0:hi> In opposition to the Spirit of God which is the <ns0:hi>Holy Spirit.</ns0:hi> The Man that had this unclean Spirit, or rather the <ns0:hi>Vnclean Spirit</ns0:hi> in the Man cryes out, <ns0:hi>Let us alone, what have we to do with thee,</ns0:hi> he doubtless feared what followed, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> That he should be cast out. He counts himself destroyed when he can<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />not do mischief like wicked Men, who are the seed of this old Serpent, who <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 4.16. <ns0:hi>Sleep not except they have done mis<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />chief, and their Sleep is taken away, unless they have made some to fall.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Devil</ns0:hi> here owneth Christ to be <ns0:hi>the Holy one of God.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="25">25 And Jesus rebuked him, saying, Hold thy peace, and come out of him.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="26">26 And when the unclean spirit had torn him, and cried with a loud voice, he came out of him.<ns0:note place="bottom">It is both here and in many other places observable, that when the Devils made a confession of Christ, yet neither Christ nor his Apostles would ever take any notice of it. Truth is never advan<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />taged from the Confession of known <ns0:hi>Lyars</ns0:hi> (as the Devil was from the beginning) Christ need not the Devils testimony, either to his <ns0:hi>Holiness,</ns0:hi> or his being <ns0:hi>the Son of God,</ns0:hi> nor would he have People allow the least faith to the Devils words. Nor was he to be imposed upon, by the Devils good words, he was to make no truce with him, but to Destroy him, and his works, he therefore chargeth him to hold his peace, and to come out, <ns0:hi>And when the Vnclean Spirit had torn him.</ns0:hi> The <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> Word here <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> is ill translated, <ns0:hi>torn,</ns0:hi> as appears by <ns0:hi>Luke</ns0:hi> 4.35. where it is said, <ns0:hi>it did him no hurt</ns0:hi>; the word signifies no more then a violent Convulsion, or shaking, and it is observed that those <ns0:hi>possessed</ns0:hi> by Devils, had only their members made use of by the Devils, but without any wound<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing or laceration of them, <ns0:hi>he cryed out with a loud voice, and came out of him.</ns0:hi> O how loth is the Devil to part with his Possession, but possibly also Christ would have him cry out with a loud Voice, that his miraculous operation, might be the more taken notice of.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="27">27 And they were all amazed, insomuch that they questioned amongst themselves, Saying, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 4.36.</ns0:note> What thing is this? what new doctrine <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> this? for with authority commandeth he even the unclean Spirits, and they do obey him?<ns0:note place="bottom">The Jews had <ns0:hi>Exorcists</ns0:hi> among<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t them, who sometimes cast out Devils, by some forms of <ns0:hi>Invocation they had,</ns0:hi> but Christ <ns0:hi>commanded them out</ns0:hi>; he neither did it, by any kind of intreaty from any compact with the Devil, nor yet <ns0:hi>by any Invocation of God,</ns0:hi> but by an <ns0:hi>Authoritative Command</ns0:hi>; this was new to the <ns0:hi>Iews,</ns0:hi> and especially confirming a new <ns0:hi>Doctrine</ns0:hi> that he had pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lished. But <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>till we read of no <ns0:hi>believing,</ns0:hi> no agnition of him as God, or the <ns0:hi>Son of God,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>Messias,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Saviour of the World,</ns0:hi> o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ly the generality are a<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>azed, they could not obtain of them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves to believe this new Doctrine, nor yet so far command their passions, but they must be startled and <ns0:hi>amazed</ns0:hi> at it.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>

               <ns0:p n="34">34 And he healed many that were sick of divers diseases, and cast out many devils, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 4.41 Acts 16, 17, 18.</ns0:note> suffered not the devils to speak <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>not to say that they knew him.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> because they knew him.<ns0:note place="bottom">It was upon the <ns0:hi>Sabbath day,</ns0:hi> (as appeareth from what went before) therefore the time is noted, <ns0:hi>at the Evening when the Sun was set.</ns0:hi> Before that time when the Sabbath was determined, the Jews thought it unlawful to carry any burdens, but after Sun-set they judged it Lawful. <ns0:hi>The usage</ns0:hi> of the Particle <ns0:hi>all</ns0:hi> here, <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 32, 33. is again observable to shew the vanity of those who will from <ns0:hi>general Particles,</ns0:hi> conclude Propositions contrary to the Analogy of Faith. I am sure <ns0:hi>Preaching</ns0:hi> was the greatest part of Christs work, how it comes to be the least part of Ministers work since<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> or how any of them think it suffi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cient to discharge that work by Journey Men, which he thought it not beneath him to do himself, may deserve their examination, which make it so; we do not say that <ns0:hi>Preaching</ns0:hi> is a greater Work then <ns0:hi>Prayer,</ns0:hi> or that it is not Ministers duty to Pray, nor yet that it is greater then <ns0:hi>administring the Sacrament.</ns0:hi> But this we say, we read of Christs Preaching o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">

                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>

                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t Work, which our Lord and his Apostles were most imployed in, and do think others will be of our Minds, assoon as they shall understand, that if the end of <ns0:hi>Preaching</ns0:hi> be not turning Men from one opinion to another, but from the love, and practice of Sin to God, there is as much need of it as ever, and that the turning of Men from one Opinion to another, without a change of heart, as to the love of Sin, is but a turning of Men from one quarter of the Devils Kingdom to another.</ns0:note>

               <ns0:p n="45">45 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Luke 5.15.</ns0:note> But he went out, and began to publish <ns0:hi>it</ns0:hi> much, and to blaze abroad the matter, insomuch that Jesus could no more openly enter into the city, but was without in desert places, and they came to him from every quarter.<ns0:note place="bottom">We before had this piece of History, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 8.2. to the Notes upon which it is enough to refer our <ns0:hi>Reader,</ns0:hi> we shall also meet with it hereafter in <ns0:hi>Luke, Ch.</ns0:hi> 5<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> Our Lord being <ns0:hi>moved with Compassion,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>affected</ns0:hi> in his <ns0:hi>Bowels,</ns0:hi> (as the Word signifies) is often used as Expressive of the cause of his <ns0:hi>Acts of Mercy</ns0:hi>; thus in curing the Leper, he at once both shewed himself the <ns0:hi>Son of Man,</ns0:hi> one who could have <ns0:hi>Compassion</ns0:hi> on <ns0:hi>our infirmities,</ns0:hi> and indeed could not but have such a <ns0:hi>Commiseration</ns0:hi> toward Mankind, and the <ns0:hi>Son of God,</ns0:hi> that he could in an instant, by a Touch, or by the Word of his Po<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
